title: This, that, and whose
title_target: これは なんですか — Kore wa nan desu ka
goal: Point at things near and far, ask what they're called in Japanese, say who owns something, and correct someone who guessed wrong.
bekal: tell これ・それ・あれ apart by distance
use この・その・あの before a noun
correct someone with ちがいます without sounding rude

dialogs.title: 会話 1 — In the classroom
dialogs.intro: Ani points at things around her and asks what they're called. Notice how the pointing words change with the distance of each thing from the two speakers.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [すみません|Sumimasen]。[これは|Kore wa] [なんですか|nan desu ka]。
lines.id: Excuse me. What is this?

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [それは|Sore wa] [じしょです|jisho desu]。[にほんごの|Nihongo no] [じしょです|jisho desu]。
lines.id: That's a dictionary. A Japanese dictionary.
lines.literal: that — as-for — dictionary — is. Japan-language — 's — dictionary — is.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [じゃあ|Jā]、[あれは|are wa]？
lines.id: Then what about that one over there?

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [あれは|Are wa] [とけいです|tokei desu]。
lines.id: That one over there is a clock.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [この|Kono] [ほんは|hon wa] [だれのですか|dare no desu ka]。
lines.id: Whose book is this?

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [それは|Sore wa] [わたしのです|watashi no desu]。
lines.id: That's mine.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [この|Kono] [ペンも|pen mo] [たなかさんのですか|Tanaka-san no desu ka]。
lines.id: Is this pen Mr. Tanaka's too?

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [いいえ|Iie]、[ちがいます|chigaimasu]。[それは|Sore wa] [やまださんのです|Yamada-san no desu]。
lines.id: No, it isn't. That's Ms. Yamada's.
lines.literal: no, differs. that — as-for — Yamada-san — 's — is.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [そうですか|Sō desu ka]。[じしょは|Jisho wa] [いくらですか|ikura desu ka]。
lines.id: I see. How much is the dictionary?
lines.literal: so — is — [question]. dictionary — as-for — how-much — is — [question]

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [ちょっと|Chotto] [たかいです|takai desu]。でも、[いい|ii] [じしょです|jisho desu]。
lines.id: A bit expensive. But it's a good dictionary.
lines.literal: a-little — expensive — is. but, good — dictionary — is.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [わたしも|Watashi mo] [ほしいです|hoshii desu]。
lines.id: I want one too.

notes: **Distance is measured from two people, not one.** これ = near the **speaker**. それ = near the **listener**. あれ = far from **both**. That's why Ani asks これは (the book in her hand) and Tanaka answers それは (the book is away from him). Two different words, the same object. Beginners often think それ means “that, a little further away”; really it means “the one on your side”.
**ちがいます is not “no” but “that's different”.** To correct someone's guess, いいえ、ちがいます is far more natural than いいえ、じゃありません. In everyday speech ちがいます often stands alone, without いいえ.
**も replaces は; it doesn't attach to it.** わたしは → わたし**も** (me too). Never write わたしはも. The same rule applies to を later: それを → それも.
**の here means “'s”.** わたしの = mine. The noun can be dropped once it's clear: それはわたしのです = “that's mine”, without repeating “book”.

**いい = good, and it's a rebel.** It's the only adjective that breaks the pattern: its negative and past forms switch to よ～ (よくない, よかった). For now just remember that いい is used as is before a noun: いいじしょ.
**ほしいです = want (to have a thing).** This differs from “want to do”, which is ～たいです — that's in Unit 9.

grammars.title: [こそあど|kosoado] — the pointing-word system
body: Japanese pointing words are neatly arranged in one grid. Once you see the grid, thirty words turn into four predictable patterns. The rows: **[こ|ko]** near me, **[そ|so]** near you, **[あ|a]** away from us both, **[ど|do]** question word.
after: ⚠️ **[これ|kore] and [この|kono] are not interchangeable.** [これ|kore] stands alone ([これはほんです|kore wa hon desu]); [この|kono] must be followed by a noun ([このほんは|kono hon wa]…). Saying [これほん|kore hon] is the most common beginner mistake you'll hear.

**[こちら|kochira] / [そちら|sochira] / [あちら|achira]** are used for directions, but also as polite versions of [これ|kore]/[それ|sore]/[あれ|are] and even to introduce people: [こちらはたなかさんです|kochira wa Tanaka-san desu] = “this is Mr. Tanaka”.

grammars.title: [の|no] — the all-purpose glue
body: The particle **[の|no]** joins two nouns: **A [の|no] B** means “B related to A”, much like English “A's B”. The word that **describes** comes first.
English: *a dictionary of Japanese* → Japanese: **[にほんごの|nihongo no] [じしょ|jisho]** (Japanese's dictionary).
This one particle covers three relationships English expresses in different ways: ownership, origin, and type.

head: Japanese
Meaning
Relationship
rows: [インドネシアの|Indoneshia no] [コーヒー|kōhī]
[にほんごの|Nihongo no] [がっこうの|gakkō no] [せんせい|sensei]
a teacher at a Japanese language school

after: **The noun can be dropped.** If the thing is clear from the conversation, just stop at [の|no]: [これはわたしのです|kore wa watashi no desu] = “this is mine”. This is the most common way to answer a [だれの|dare no] question.
**Asking:** [だれの|dare no] = whose. [このかばんはだれのですか|kono kaban wa dare no desu ka] = “whose bag is this?”

dialogs.title: 会話 2 — Lost property
dialogs.intro: At the front desk, someone is looking for a bag they left behind. Notice how people correct and how they confirm.

lines.speaker: うけつけ:
lines.text: [はい|Hai]、[うけつけです|uketsuke desu]。
lines.id: Yes, front desk.

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [すみません|Sumimasen]。[かばんを|Kaban o] [わすれました|wasuremashita]。
lines.id: Excuse me. I left my bag behind.

lines.speaker: うけつけ:
lines.text: [どんな|Donna] [かばんですか|kaban desu ka]。
lines.id: What kind of bag is it?

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [くろい|Kuroi] [かばんです|kaban desu]。[なかに|Naka ni] [パソコンが|pasokon ga] [あります|arimasu]。
lines.id: A black bag. There's a laptop inside.
lines.literal: black — bag — is. inside — in — computer — [subject] — exists.

lines.speaker: うけつけ:
lines.text: [これですか|Kore desu ka]。
lines.id: Is it this one?

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [いいえ|Iie]、[ちがいます|chigaimasu]。[それは|Sore wa] [わたしのじゃありません|watashi no ja arimasen]。
lines.id: No, it isn't. That's not mine.
lines.literal: no, differs. that — as-for — I — 's — is-not.

lines.speaker: うけつけ:
lines.text: [じゃあ|Jā]、[あれは|are wa] [どうですか|dō desu ka]。
lines.id: Then how about that one over there?

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [あ|A]、[そうです|sō desu]！[あれです|Are desu]。[わたしのです|Watashi no desu]。
lines.id: Ah, yes! That's it. It's mine.
lines.literal: ah, so — is! that-over-there — is. I — 's — is.

lines.speaker: うけつけ:
lines.text: [おなまえは|Onamae wa]？
lines.id: Your name?

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [ブディです|Budi desu]。[インドネシアの|Indoneshia no] [がくせいです|gakusei desu]。
lines.id: Budi. I'm a student from Indonesia.

lines.speaker: うけつけ:
lines.text: [はい|Hai]、[どうぞ|dōzo]。
lines.id: All right, here you are.

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [たすかりました|Tasukarimashita]。[ありがとうございます|Arigatō gozaimasu]。
lines.id: You've saved me. Thank you very much.

notes: **どんな = “what kind of”**, always followed by a noun: どんなかばん, どんなひと, どんなくるま. Don't confuse it with どう (= how), which stands alone: どうですか.
**どうですか has two jobs:** asking for an opinion (“what do you think?”) and offering (“how about this one?”). In this dialogue it's the second.

**どうぞ = please / here you are**, used when handing something over, inviting someone to sit, or letting them go first. Its partner is どうも, which can be a short “thanks”. Two similar words, two opposite directions.
**たすかりました literally means “I was saved”** and is a warmer thank-you than a plain ありがとう — perfect when someone has really rescued you from trouble.
**が and あります make a brief appearance here.** Both are fully explained in Unit 5. For now, read ～があります as one package meaning “there is ～”.
**くろい = black**, one of the い-adjectives that can go straight in front of a noun: くろいかばん. Adjectives are covered fully in Unit 7.

grammars.title: [も|mo] — “also”, and what it pushes out
body: **[も|mo]** means “also / too”, and it **replaces** the particle [は|wa] or [を|o] instead of attaching after it.
[わたしはがくせいです|watashi wa gakusei desu]。→ [ブディさん|Budi-san]**[も|mo]**[がくせいです|gakusei desu]。 (Budi is a student too.)
In a negative sentence, [も|mo] means “not … either”: [わたしもがくせいじゃありません|watashi mo gakusei ja arimasen] = “I'm not a student either”.

head: Original sentence
With も
Meaning
rows: [わたしは|watashi wa] [がくせいです|gakusei desu]
[わたしも|watashi mo] [がくせいです|gakusei desu]
[これは|kore wa] [わたしのです|watashi no desu]
[これも|kore mo] [わたしのです|watashi no desu]

after: ⚠️ The most common mistake: writing **[わたしはも|watashi wa mo]**. There's only one particle — choose [は|wa] or [も|mo], not both.

grammars.title: Correcting without sounding rude
body: Japanese has its own ladder of politeness for saying “no”. Picking the wrong rung is one of the fastest ways to sound stiff.

head: Expression
Feel
Used when
rows: Correcting a fact: someone guessed wrong.
Answering a yes/no question. Rarely stands alone.
Declining an invitation or request without saying no.
Correcting someone older or a superior.
[そうじゃないです|sō ja nai desu]

after: **A trailing [ちょっと|chotto]… is a refusal.** If you invite a Japanese person and the answer is “[ちょっと|chotto]…”, it means no — not “just a moment”. Waiting for the rest of the sentence is a very common misunderstanding.

blocks.text: Most modern objects in Japan use loanwords written in katakana. Once you can read katakana, you already know these words before memorizing them — try guessing before you look at the right-hand column.
And here are everyday things that **don't** use loanwords — these you'll have to learn:

sections.title: Check before you get it wrong

blocks.text: Everyday conversation is more about checking than stating. These three short patterns cover almost everything a beginner needs:

head: Pattern
Example
Meaning
rows: [それは|Sore wa] [わたしのですよ|watashi no desu yo]。

blocks.title: ね and よ — the two tiniest words that change the tone most
items: **ね** invites agreement: “right?”. It softens the sentence. When in doubt, ね almost always improves your tone.
**よ** tells the listener something they don't know yet: “you know”. Useful, but overusing it can sound preachy.
**Without either**, a sentence sounds flat and a little cold — like reading a list. Not wrong, but distant.
